ny_e_high_peaks_region.blurb: The High Peaks Region is the Adirondack backcountry of northern New York, where climbing means real commitment rather than roadside cragging. The rock is anorthosite, which climbs much like granite. The mix is broad: trad leads make up nearly half of the climbs, alongside scrambles, alpine lines, winter ice, boulder problems and only a handful of bolted routes. Most trad grades sit between 5.7 and 5.10, with a thinner tail up to 5.12, and the ice runs mainly WI3 to WI5. Approaches are measured in miles and often involve bushwhacking. Big slabby faces such as the north side of Gothics approach a thousand feet, and the climbing there is runout and demanding to navigate. Panther Gorge, Wallface and Ragged Mountain are among the larger sub-areas. Expect solitude, patchy phone coverage and a slow rescue if things go wrong.

_expect.name: Boulders on Old Wauhatchie Pike, The

tn_boulders_on_old_wauhatchie_pike_the.blurb: These boulders sit at the foot of Lookout Mountain beside Chattanooga's St. Elmo neighborhood, close to downtown, in a fifty-acre park set aside for bouldering. Everything here is bouldering: 27 boulders carry well over two hundred problems. Difficulty covers the whole range. Easy V0 to V2 problems are plentiful, the middle grades from V3 to V6 are well represented, and a small group of hard problems reaches V8 and beyond. Trails and built-up landings make for quick, convenient sessions, so it suits an after-work visit or a group of mixed ability. The Cliffhanger, Asteroid and Hermanos Cercanos are among the larger clusters.

ut_left_fork_2.blurb: Left Fork is one of the busiest arms of Joe's Valley, a sandstone bouldering destination in central Utah near Orangeville, east of the reservoir. The boulders sit at roughly 6,500 feet, and well over two hundred problems are spread across twenty-plus zones. Grades run from V0 up to V13, with most between V2 and V8, so moderate climbers and strong ones both have plenty to do. Riverside is the favorite for easier problems and Big Joe next door draws heavy traffic, while Mine Cart Area and Right Sign Area are among the largest zones. Sandstone loses much of its strength when wet, so climbers leave the rock alone for a couple of days after rain.

wa_miller_river_boulders.blurb: Miller River Boulders lies in the Skykomish Valley of Washington's Central-West Cascades, in a junglelike valley with an old mining past. The rock is granodiorite and all of the climbing is bouldering. Grades cover everything from V0 to V13, with the greatest numbers between V2 and V6. Seven sectors share the valley. Morpheus alone holds about half of the problems, along the former mine road beside the West Fork, mixing sunny talus with shaded devil's club forest, riverside blocs and trailside ones. It offers crimpy test pieces next to friendly moderates. Paradise, Prospect and Hideout are the other larger sectors. The valley is quieter and less developed than neighboring bouldering areas, though river crossings, bushwhacking and seasonal talus fields can make some blocs a chore to reach.

nv_lake_tahoe_area.blurb: The Nevada side of Lake Tahoe stretches from Crystal Bay and Incline Village on the north shore round to the Stateline area in the south, with climbing scattered across many small crags and boulder fields rather than one big cliff. Bouldering is the most numerous, followed by sport and then trad, with a few top-rope lines. Sport routes run mainly from 5.6 to 5.12, with the biggest cluster around 5.10 and 5.11. Castle Rock is the largest crag: mostly bolted sport, about half of it moderate, vertical and often jugged, with lake views and a main wall facing south. Trippy Rock near Incline Village is a compact 75-foot wall of sport and top-rope lines with a few boulder problems. Spooner Crag and the Zephyrs boulders are other larger sub-areas.

nc_dixon_school_boulders.blurb: Dixon School Boulders is a bouldering-only field in the Crowders Mountain area of North Carolina's Piedmont. The boulders are metamorphosed quartz-pebble conglomerate, folded into a broad arch, with the white pebbles stretched long by pressure. Holds come from weathering along the rock's layering, plus fractures and flakes peeling off the surface. Grades run from V0 to V10, but most problems sit between V0 and V4, which suits newer boulderers while leaving a few hard lines. The field is split into a lower section and an Upper Dixon that follows the main boulder trail to the northeast and includes some aretes. Larger zones include Upper Dixon, Patio Area and Old Folks Home.
